name: context ceiling — step -c upward to the spill tipping point

derived_from.launcher: none — the .ps1 builds the llama-server argv itself

notes: RECONSTRUCTION (read this before trusting a number from these arms). ctx-limit-sweep.ps1, sweep-efforts.ps1, sweep-pass2.ps1 and sweep-tune.ps1 call serve-qwen.bat WITHOUT the model argument, so they took whatever the menu's default was on the day. The shipped stand-in scripts/reference-3090/serve-menu-example.bat defaults to entry [1] (UD-IQ4_XS), but it was re-measured at the END of the campaign; four independent sources say the default these scripts actually took was entry [4] (Q4_K_M + projector, -c 122880, 'quality champion, reference config'): (a) reference-3090/README.md maps ctx-limit-sweep.ps1 to Q4_K_M and iq4-ctx-sweep.ps1 to IQ4_XS; (b) iq4-ctx-sweep.ps1's own header treats Q4_K_M's ceiling as ALREADY measured ('Q4_K_M measured ~131k resident / ~213k shallow'); (c) sweep-efforts.ps1 and sweep-tune.ps1 hardcode $modelName = 'Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M' for their output files; (d) templates/example-report.html publishes the Q4_K_M ceiling as '~131k resident, about 213,000 before the server refuses to start' with the projector loaded — and 212,992 is exactly rung 11 of this file's +8192 ladder. Entry [4] is therefore reconstructed, not read off the .bat.

TWO SWEEPS, ONE FILE: q4km-ceiling ran first (ctx-limit-sweep.ps1), iq4xs-ceiling later (iq4-ctx-sweep.ps1) with a DIFFERENT flag set — the IQ4 script launches llama-server directly and passes no sampler flags, no --reasoning-preserve, no --chat-template-kwargs and no --image-min-tokens. rule 30: arms are only comparable INSIDE one sweep. The "sweep" field on each arm names which sweep it belongs to; never put an absolute t/s from one sweep beside one from another.
Every arm's flags are COMPLETE and self-contained: nothing is inherited from "defaults", so a runner that ignores "defaults" still launches the exact server the reference campaign launched.

"mmproj" after --mmproj is a LOGICAL model name, resolved through paths.model_path() exactly like server.model (arms.py MODEL_FLAGS resolves it into the argv and leaves the arm's flag list logical, so the resume hash does not depend on where this machine keeps its weights). No absolute path appears in this file — erasing the author-machine lmstudio/models paths is the point of the port. Stage 0 must map every name in "models" below into campaign.json.

GREEDY IS THE MEASUREMENT: every probe in these .ps1 files posted temperature=0 and top_k=1 in the request body and nothing else, so that is what each probe here declares. arms.py sends exactly the sampler a probe names and injects no default of its own; a probe that named none would inherit the server's --temp 1.0 and stop being a comparison. The values are repeated in "defaults" as well, but every probe carries its own — an arm read in isolation still states the conditions it was measured under (rule 3).

Dropped from every flag list, deliberately and identically: --api-key dummy (access control, not measurement — scripts/probe-config.sh, this repo's POSIX seed, drops it too) and --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 (the runner owns the transport, exactly as scripts/bench/bench.py's Server injects them). Nothing else was dropped, reordered or retyped.

rule 12: these arms carry repeat=1 / discard_first=false because that is what ran. A rerun that wants the clock-ramp protocol raises repeat and sets discard_first — and is then a NEW sweep, not comparable arm-by-arm with the published numbers (rule 30).

SHALLOW PROBE ONLY: a 400-token code probe on a freshly loaded server never touches the deep pages, so this ladder finds the SHALLOW-SAFE ceiling and the load-failure point — not the fully-resident one. Rule 13: no window is labeled without a deep-fill probe near its top. Take the deep-fill probe from depth-series.json.

THE LADDER IS DERIVED, NOT WRITTEN HERE (rule 1). Each of the two arms below is a TEMPLATE: arms.py expands it into one arm per rung of results/<slug>/plan.json, which scripts/plan-campaign.py derives from this file's own GGUF header (context_length, KV bytes/token, weights) and this machine's machine.json (board total, desktop reserve). The rule it uses travels in that file as rungs.step_rule and is printed by --dry-run. Run `python scripts/plan-campaign.py --slug <slug>` first; without a plan this file ABORTS and names that command. There is no fallback, deliberately: a ceiling belongs to ⟨file + card⟩, and until 2026-08-29 this file hardcoded 25 arms at 18 distinct -c values from 122,880 to 262,144, every one of them sized for one 27B on one 24 GB card.

WHAT THE HARDCODED LADDER WAS, AND WHERE IT WENT. "rungs".reference_rungs on each arm below holds the exact -c list that arm used to carry — q4km-ceiling 18 rungs at +8,192 from 122,880 to 262,144, iq4xs-ceiling 7 rungs over the same span — kept as DATA rather than prose so --dry-run can compare it against the ladder this machine derives and print REPRODUCED or DIFFERENT. How many rungs a machine gets is not fixed and is not asserted here: it falls out of the fit, and a model whose whole window is resident gets ONE rung because there is no ceiling to find. Read the ladder off --dry-run before committing the hours. Numbers measured on a different ladder are not arm-for-arm comparable with the published ones (rule 30).

THE ARM IDS ARE GENERATED: "q4km-mmproj-c{rung.c}" becomes q4km-mmproj-c122880 and so on, one per rung, ascending. They key the ledger and the resume index, so they change when the plan changes — which is correct: a rung derived for another card is another arm. `--only` takes the EXPANDED id; `--list` prints them.

stop_rule.reference_arm: the LOWEST rung of each sweep — the first arm in file order, because the plan emits rungs in ascending -c. In the reference campaign that arm was the one named -ref (-c 122880); under a derived ladder it is whatever the bottom rung is on this machine, and the ledger's ctx_size records which. Note what that does to the floor: the reference campaign took its 0.75x floor against a 122,880-token window, and a derived ladder takes it against its own bottom rung, which is a lever rung far below the ceiling and therefore FASTER. The floor is stricter, which is the behaviour a ceiling hunt wants — but the two floors are different numbers and the walks are not comparable arm for arm (rule 30).
stop_rule.floor: 0.75 x the reference arm's t/s (ctx-limit-sweep.ps1: $floor = round($refTps * 0.75, 1))
stop_rule.fail_is_over_the_limit: a server that never becomes healthy counts as 0 t/s, i.e. below the floor
stop_rule.walk: run the rungs in file order; STOP at the first rung below the floor. Every later rung in the ladder is the generator's continuation, not a measurement the reference campaign made — the .ps1 breaks out of the loop at the first bad rung.
stop_rule.then: binary-refine between the last good and the first bad rung at 4096-token resolution (mid = floor((good+bad)/2 / 4096) * 4096). That step is DATA-DEPENDENT and cannot be declared here: run it with `--only` one arm at a time, or add the refined rungs to this file as LITERAL arms beside the templates — an arm with no "rungs" object keeps whatever -c it names, and a file may mix the two.

record: per probe: completion tokens, wall seconds, server timings (prompt_n, prompt_per_second, prompt_ms, predicted_n, predicted_per_second)
per probe: draft_n and draft_n_accepted -> acceptance AND mean draft length (rule 11 — publish both)
per arm: dedicated VRAM MiB, sampled while the probe runs (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv,noheader,nounits)
per arm: regime (thinking/answer), depth, cap, desktop state, RAM channels (rule 3) — written the moment it exists, never buffered (rule 28)

arms.derived_from: ctx-limit-sweep.ps1 via serve-menu-example.bat [4], effort low — flags verbatim, -c DERIVED per machine (see "rungs")
